methods.name: Behavioral Methods
methods.definition: Behavioral methods examine models at the level of inputs and outputs: capability evaluations (Linzen et al., 2016; Marvin & Linzen, 2018; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), deceptive intents (Kinniment et al., 2026), and red-teaming (Ganguli et al., 2022; Perez et al., 2022b; He et al., 2025).
assumptions: These approaches are fast, scalable, and practical for high-level auditing without access to model internals.
applications: Behavioral methods nonetheless remain essential in practice, for rapid iteration during development, for prioritizing which behaviors warrant deeper investigation, and for surface-level safety screening where the cost of mechanistic analysis is prohibitive.
limitations: The limits of this approach are the subject of Section 2; the point that matters here is that behaviour on a finite evaluation set underdetermines the mechanism that produced it, which is what the internal methods below are designed to establish.
These studies assess what models do without explaining how.

methods.name: Concept-Based Approaches (Concept Bottleneck Models)
methods.definition: Concept-based methods plays a middle ground role: they go beyond behavioral evaluation by examining internal representations, but typically establish correlational rather than causal claims.
assumptions: CBMs impose semantic constraints (predefined human concepts), while architectural interventions impose structural constraints (sparsity, modularity) that allow the model to discover features autonomously.
applications: These methods do not guarantee mechanistic understanding but are valuable for auditing, localization, and early detection tasks.

Practical Guide: CBMs tend to be more appropriate when the relevant concepts are known and can be enumerated; architectural interventions may be preferable when the goal is to discover what the model has learned—including features that were not known in advance.
limitations: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs; Koh et al., 2020) constrain computation through a predefined bottleneck of interpretable concepts, offering built-in transparency and allowing for interventions, but traditionally requiring a complete set of predefined concepts and often suffer from an “accuracy-interpretability trade-off” when concept definitions are insufficiently expressive.
For safety applications, where unknown failure modes are a core concern, methods that enable discovery may be more useful than those that require specifying concepts upfront.

methods.name: Attribution and Saliency Methods
methods.definition: Attribution methods focus on identifying which features most influence a model’s outputs. Techniques such as SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017), LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016), integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017), and saliency maps (Simonyan et al., 2014) are scalable and widely used for token-level explanations and debugging.
evaluation: However, Jacovi & Goldberg (2020) distinguish between plausibility (do attributions seem reasonable to humans?) and faithfulness (do attributions reflect actual model computation?).
applications: For the safety-relevant tasks motivating this survey, attribution methods are useful for triage and initial auditing but, on their own, insufficient where a causal account of internal computation is required.
limitations: Applied to inputs, they indicate which inputs matter but not how the model arrives at its output.

Reliability concerns nonetheless remain: different attribution methods can produce divergent explanations for the same prediction, and some have been shown to be insensitive to model parameters (Adebayo et al., 2018b).
Collectively, these findings suggest that attribution methods are fundamentally unreliable guides to what information a model actually uses.

methods.name: Probing Classifiers
methods.definition: A probe trains a classifier—typically linear—to predict a property (e.g., part-of-speech, sentiment, entity type) from model activations.
assumptions: Linear probes constrain g to be linear, testing whether the property is linearly accessible.
MLP probes allow nonlinear g, testing whether the property is present in any recoverable form.
evaluation: A control task assigns random labels to inputs, breaking any genuine relationship between activations and the target property.
High selectivity indicates the probe succeeds because of genuine encoding, not because the representation is easily separable by any linear classifier.
To address this, Voita & Titov (2020) proposed evaluating probes via the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle: prefer probes that achieve good accuracy with minimal complexity.
Report control task baselines: Always include selectivity metrics.
applications: probes have become one of the most widely used tools in mechanistic interpretability for tasks including layer-level localization, scalable auditing, and detecting latent behaviors such as sleeper-agent deception (MacDiarmid et al., 2024).

The most productive framing treats probing as hypothesis generation: probes identify candidate properties that may be causally relevant, which must then be tested via causal methods (ablation, patching, circuit analysis).
This illustrates that probing remains valuable when the goal is auditing or detection, while its limitations apply most strongly to mechanistic claims.
limitations: Probing does not establish causal relevance: whether the model actually uses that information for its predictions.
This problem is fundamental: probing measures information presence, not information use.

Control task experiments have revealed that many probing results showing “encoding” of linguistic properties suffer from low selectivity—random labels are nearly as extractable (Hewitt & Liang, 2019).

methods.name: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs)
methods.definition: Sparse Autoencoders are a way of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic neurons.
assumptions: They are optimised for accuracy to the real MLP or attention block and for having few active features for any given forward pass.
SAEs are motivated by the hypothesis that features occur sparsely in the data and are linearly recoverable from a model’s hidden states.
Training of SAEs is sensitive to initialization, sparsity strength, and decoder normalization.
evaluation: SAEs are typically evaluated for reconstruction loss (fidelity of activation reconstruction), feature absorption (degree to which features remain distinct), and downstream testing loss recovery (whether replacing activations with reconstructions preserves model behavior).
Report failure mode metrics: Alongside reconstruction loss, report dead feature percentage, duplication rate (via cosine similarity), and stability across seeds.
These causal tests should be standard practice when claiming that SAE features represent meaningful computational units.
applications: As a result, supervised methods are best suited to settings where specific, predefined concepts are of interest, such as safety-critical behaviors like toxicity or deception, whereas SAEs remain preferable for exploratory analysis.
SAEs to unsupervisedly discover monosemantic features inside the model’s raw activations.
limitations: Dead features represent wasted capacity and can constitute between 10–50% of the dictionary in poorly tuned SAEs (Bricken et al., 2023).
Training the same architecture with different random seeds can therefore produce substantially different dictionaries (Paulo & Belrose, 2025).
Taken together, these behaviors are consistent with the failure of identifiability under high-coherence conditions and help explain why SAE features can be unstable, non-atomic, and seed-dependent.
Low SAE reconstruction loss does not necessarily mean that SAE captures the causal structure of the original model.

methods.name: Gated SAEs
methods.definition: Gated SAEs introduce multiplicative gates to decouple feature selection from magnitude
applications: Recommendation: Use Gated SAE as the default unless you have specific reasons for standard.
Standard SAEs suffer from shrinkage bias; Gated SAEs solve this with minimal added complexity.

methods.name: JumpReLU SAEs
methods.definition: JumpReLU SAEs learn per-feature activation thresholds.
assumptions: A smooth surrogate is used during training to enable gradient flow Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b).

methods.name: Top-k SAEs
methods.definition: Top-k SAEs (Gao et al., 2025a) impose an explicit hard sparsity constraint.
assumptions: No sparsity penalty needed; sparsity is enforced structurally.
evaluation: Unlike L1 loss, it does not suppress activation magnitudes, thereby avoiding the feature shrinkage issue observed in L1-based SAE training (Gao et al., 2025a).
applications: If you’re spending significant time tuning the sparsity coefficient, Top-K eliminates this hyperparameter entirely.

methods.name: Batch Top-k SAEs
methods.definition: Batch Top-k SAEs enforce sparsity at the batch level.
applications: This enforces global feature competition, reduces variance in feature usage across the batch, and prevents collapse (Bussmann et al., 2024).
More recent Batch Top-K variants explicitly enforce minimum feature usage across batches, which substantially reduces the prevalence of dead features (Bussmann et al., 2024).

methods.name: Transcoders
methods.definition: The transcoder reconstructs post-nonlinearity activations using features extracted from pre-nonlinearity activations (Dunefsky et al., 2024).
assumptions: A transcoder applies sparse decomposition directly to the nonlinear mapping, learning features that explain the transformation.
applications: Transcoders are essential when analyzing MLPs, understanding feature interactions, or tracking how concepts evolve across layers (Dunefsky et al., 2024).
Recommendation: For MLP analysis, use transcoders; for cross-layer analysis, use crosscoders or CLTs.
limitations: Transcoders improve this by imitating the behavior of the MLP, revealing nonlinear transformations, though they require sequential analysis across depth.

methods.name: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs)
methods.definition: A Cross-Layer Transcoder (CLT) is a sparse feature decomposition spanning all layers of a neural network.
assumptions: Attention freezing: By caching attention patterns, the replacement model treats attention as a fixed routing operation rather than a dynamic, input-dependent computation.
Normalization caching: Freezing LayerNorm statistics removes a source of nonlinearity but introduces dependence on the specific input used to cache these statistics.

Sparse linear approximation: The core assumption that MLP outputs are well-approximated by sparse linear combinations of features may break down for computations involving complex feature interactions or highly nonlinear transformations.
evaluation: Empirically, CLT replacement models match the original model’s most-likely token on approximately 50% of prompts in initial experiments on Gemma-2-2B (Ameisen et al., 2025).
The 50% figure reflects top-1 token agreement; softer metrics (e.g., top-5 agreement, KL divergence) may show different patterns.

These caveats do not invalidate CLTs as a tool for mechanistic analysis, but practitioners should verify fidelity on their specific model, layer, and task before drawing strong conclusions from CLT-based circuit analysis.
applications: A key insight is that CLTs enable the construction of a replacement model: a version of the original model where all MLP layers are replaced by their CLT reconstructions.
This simplifies circuit structure—features need not re-encode information at each layer.
When these assumptions hold, CLTs provide a powerful lens for circuit discovery.
limitations: When they fail, particularly for complex reasoning or out-of-distribution inputs, CLT-based explanations may be incomplete or misleading.
Training a CLT requires significant upfront cost, which scales with the number of features and layers.
This scarcity of downstream applications in the current literature likely reflects the considerable challenges in training CLTs at scale.
Cross-layer transcoders span multiple layers for global information flow but are extremely expensive.

methods.name: Crosscoders
methods.definition: Crosscoders resolve cross-layer superposition by tracking features that persist through the residual stream (Lindsey et al., 2024).
applications: By extracting cross-layer features, crosscoders enable understanding how features propagate through the residual stream across layers, removing duplicate feature representations that complicate circuit analysis.
Crosscoders can define model-specific encoders, with arbitrarily different input dimensions, which then project into one or more shared representational spaces.
limitations: This can result from the loss function: for instance, Minder et al. (2025) showed that crosscoders trained with an L1 loss on hidden states can falsely identify novel features, which they try to mitigate with the BatchTopK activation function.

methods.name: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
methods.definition: This constraint induces a natural parts-based interpretation in which features combine additively without cancellation.
assumptions: Activations produced by modern architectures, particularly after LayerNorm or nonlinearities such as GELU, are not naturally non-negative, requiring preprocessing steps that may distort representational structure.
evaluation: Shafran et al. (2025) showed that Semi-NMF can recover features competitive with SAEs on small-scale evaluations, but systematic comparisons at large scale remain limited.
limitations: Moreover, NMF does not explicitly encourage sparsity unless additional regularization is introduced, and scaling NMF to large dictionaries is computationally challenging.

methods.name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
methods.definition: Principal Component Analysis decomposes activations by finding an orthonormal basis of directions that maximise explained variance.
assumptions: In addition, PCA enforces orthogonality between components, a constraint that may not reflect how features are organized in practice, where factors can be correlated or partially overlapping.
evaluation: In Wu et al. (2025), PCA underperforms most baselines, including SAEs, on both steering and concept-detection evaluations.
While in some localization settings, PCA outperform SAEs (Mueller et al., 2025a), it still lags behind simpler supervised baselines.
applications: Missing baselines: Claims of interpretability gains rarely compare against simple baselines (e.g., random directions, PCA components, raw neurons).
limitations: PCA identifies a single set of global directions that maximises variance across the full activation distribution, which can mix multiple sources of variation when the relevant structure is region or context-dependent.

methods.name: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
methods.definition: Independent Component Analysis seeks to decompose activations as H = WS, where the components of S are statistically independent (Hyvärinen & Oja, 2000).
assumptions: However, ICA makes strong assumptions that are often violated in neural representations.
Classical ICA assumes a complete setting in which the number of sources equals the dimensionality of the representation, and extensions are required for overcomplete decompositions.
Unlike SAEs, ICA does not require tuning a sparsity hyperparameter.
limitations: Although ICA has been applied to neural network activations (Hyvärinen et al., 2023), it has not matched the interpretability gains reported for SAEs in recent large-scale studies, possibly because neural features tend to be sparse rather than independent.

methods.name: Supervised Feature Extraction Methods (DAS, SMDS, DBM)
methods.definition: When the concepts of interest are known in advance, supervised methods can directly optimize representations aligned with those targets.
assumptions: However, these methods require labelled data for each concept and therefore cannot discover previously unknown features.
evaluation: When labelled data are available, supervised approaches often outperform SAEs on targeted concept recovery tasks (Huang et al., 2024; Chaudhary & Geiger, 2024).
applications: As a result, supervised methods are best suited to settings where specific, predefined concepts are of interest, such as safety-critical behaviors like toxicity or deception, whereas SAEs remain preferable for exploratory analysis.
Compare methods: For safety-critical applications, compare SAE features against supervised baselines (DAS, probes) to assess whether SAEs recover the relevant structure.
limitations: They do not scale naturally to open-ended exploration across entire models, and each concept typically requires separate training.

methods.name: Dictionary Learning Baselines (K-SVD)
methods.definition: Classical dictionary learning methods provide useful baselines for evaluating SAEs. Techniques such as K-SVD alternate between sparse coding and dictionary updates and are known to converge under certain conditions (Aharon et al., 2006).
evaluation: Comparative studies suggest that the primary advantage of SAEs lies in their learned encoder, which enables fast inference, rather than in fundamentally superior dictionary quality (Cunningham et al., 2023).
applications: As such, classical dictionary learning remains an important reference point for assessing the added value of SAE architectures.

methods.name: Weight-Sparse Transformer (Weight Sparsity via L_0 Regularization)
methods.definition: The most significant recent advancement is the Weight-Sparse Transformer, introduced by Gao et al. (Gao et al., 2025b). This approach treats sparsity not as a tool for inference efficiency but as a tool for circuit discovery.
assumptions: Since the L_0 norm is non-differentiable, training employs stochastic gates drawn from a Hard-Concrete distribution, allowing gradients to flow while penalizing the probability of each gate being open.
Furthermore, this approach requires training sparse models from scratch or using Bridge proxies—it cannot be directly applied to existing dense models.
evaluation: Validation via mean ablation shows that these sparse circuits satisfy necessity and sufficiency criteria with higher precision than circuits identified in dense models.
Empirically, sparse circuits satisfy necessity and sufficiency criteria with higher precision than circuits extracted from dense models via post-hoc methods (Gao et al., 2025b; Haider et al., 2025).
applications: Circuits can be identified by simply visualizing non-zero weights connected to a target output, eliminating the need for activation patching or ACDC.
limitations: Weight sparsity does not eliminate all challenges.
Circuits may still be compositional (requiring understanding of how subcircuits interact), and the interpretability of individual neurons depends on training dynamics.
Retraining frontier models with sparsity constraints is computationally prohibitive.

methods.name: Sparse Attention Post-Training (SPARTAN)
methods.definition: Sparse Attention Post-Training (SPARTAN) applies L_1 regularization to the attention patterns while finetuning with a constrained optimization objective to maintain the same cross-entropy performance (Draye et al., 2025) (Lei et al., 2025).
applications: This reveals that much attention connectivity is redundant noise, and SPARTAN effectively performs circuit discovery by pruning the attention graph.
Using Cross-Layer Transcoders, they show that the reduced number of mediating components renders attention attribution tractable.

methods.name: Softmax Linear Units (SoLU)
methods.definition: Softmax Linear Units (SoLU) replace element-wise activations with a spatial softmax (Elhage et al., 2022b)
assumptions: This forces neurons within a layer to compete: if one neuron fires strongly, it suppresses its neighbors through lateral inhibition.
evaluation: SoLU successfully increased the fraction of monosemantic neurons identifiable by human inspection.
limitations: However, it revealed a critical limitation: the hydraulic effect.

When prevented from using neurons for superposition, models simply displaced the compression elsewhere—into the residual stream, into sub-threshold activations, or into other components not subject to the constraint.
This indicates that local architectural constraints are insufficient when global incentives for compression remain.

methods.name: Sparse Mixtures of Linear Transforms (MOLT)
methods.definition: One recent example of this is the so-called Sparse Mixtures of Linear Transforms (MOLT), representing a conceptual shift from feature extraction to transformation extraction (Lindsey et al., 2025b).
assumptions: MOLT replaces the MLP with a sparse mixture of linear transformation matrices.
applications: For modular arithmetic, a MOLT might learn a single rotation matrix implementing addition, rather than memorizing thousands of input-output pairs.

This aligns the architecture with the true algorithmic structure of the task, yielding higher mechanistic faithfulness than standard feature-based decompositions for tasks involving systematic transformations.

methods.name: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs)
methods.definition: Based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, KANs place learnable activation functions (B-splines) on edges rather than fixed activations on nodes.
applications: Because non-linearities are univariate and visible on edges, researchers can perform symbolic regression on learned splines to recover exact mathematical formulas—for instance, rediscovering physics equations from data.
limitations: While currently slower to train and unproven at LLM scale, KANs represent the ambitious ideal of a model where weights are interpretable mathematical functions.

methods.name: The Bridge Methodology
methods.definition: A Bridge is a weight-sparse model trained to mimic the internal representations of a pretrained dense model—minimizing reconstruction error of layer-wise activations rather than training on the original task.
evaluation: Preliminary evidence suggests that interventions on sparse proxies (e.g., ablating identified circuits) can be mapped back to induce similar behavioral changes in dense models.

One approach is causal correspondence testing, which verifies that ablating a circuit in the proxy and the corresponding components in the dense model produces matched behavioral changes across different inputs.
applications: Retraining frontier models with sparsity constraints is computationally prohibitive.
limitations: However, validating proxy fidelity—ensuring the proxy captures the same mechanisms rather than behaviorally equivalent simulations—remains an open problem (see Section 15).

methods.name: Activation Patching
methods.definition: Activation patching evaluates the causal contribution of a component or set of components S by replacing their activations with baseline values
evaluation: Perform activation patching: swap C between clean and corrupted inputs; verify behavior follows C.
applications: This identifies which components are functionally necessary for the computation (Zhang & Nanda, 2024).

A probe might detect deceptive reasoning, but confirming the finding is causal, and designing targeted interventions, requires causal intervention on internal representations—whether through activation patching, steering, or ablation.
Causal spot-checks: Randomly sample agentic explanations and verify via causal interventions, such as activation patching.
limitations: Confounds correlation with causation

methods.name: Path Patching
methods.definition: Path patching extends attribution to specific paths or edges in the computation graph.
applications: This allows finer-grained causal localization along information flows (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023).
limitations: Computationally expensive due to large number of paths; still approximate

methods.name: ACDC
methods.definition: ACDC identifies minimal sufficient sets of components S \subseteq \text{Graph}(\text{model}) that reproduce the model’s behavior.
evaluation: Scales better due to automation; has been proved to recover known circuits
limitations: Computationally expensive as it greedily prunes paths; misses subtle components

methods.name: Circuit Tracing (SAE- or CLT-Integrated circuit discovery)
methods.definition: The second line of work, often referred to as circuit tracing, focuses on how internal features interact and propagate across the computational graph to lead to the model decision of a particular input query (Ameisen et al., 2025; Wu & Barez, 2025).
assumptions: Studies of this line usually make use of sparse autoencoders (detailed in Section 6) to automatically decompose mlp outputs into interpretable units, tracing attributions between these features and how the information flow converges to the final prediction.
applications: Stage 2 – Circuit Tracing: We construct a computational graph in which nodes correspond to activated SAE features and edges represent their inter-attributions (Marks et al., 2025a).
limitations: Depends on feature quality; intensive computation to train SAEs/CLTs

methods.name: Causal Scrubbing
methods.definition: Causal scrubbing evaluates necessity by replacing circuit activations with corrupted or neutralized values and measuring the resulting change in model outputs.
evaluation: Two widely used high-level methods for testing these properties are causal scrubbing and interchange interventions (Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024; Chan et al., 2022).
applications: Circuit faithfulness: proving circuits are necessary and sufficient for explaining behavior via causal intervention (e.g., causal scrubbing), without performance degradation.
limitations: Strict necessity and sufficiency are often unattainable.

Additionally, verification assumes the circuit mechanism is faithfully captured by the identified components, but if features are entangled or nonlinear interactions are present, the measured circuit may not reflect true causal structure.

methods.name: Interchange Interventions
methods.definition: Interchange interventions test sufficiency by swapping circuit components between clean and corrupted forward passes and assessing whether the target behavior consistently tracks the substituted circuit across inputs.
applications: Test causal relevance: Complement probing with amnesic probing or interchange interventions.
limitations: This provides stronger evidence than amnesic probing but requires identifying the specific representation component, not just demonstrating its existence.

methods.name: Logit Lens
methods.definition: Logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the model’s unembedding matrix to activations at intermediate layers, revealing what the model would predict if computation stopped at that layer.
assumptions: Applying the unembedding matrix to intermediate activations assumes that the hidden state is in a format the output layer expects, but intermediate representations may reside in vector spaces different from final activations.
applications: By examining this trajectory, researchers can identify at which layer critical decisions emerge: whether the model commits early to a prediction or progressively refines it layer-by-layer.
In this sense, logit lens can still reveal contributions to potentially harmful tokens and track how these emerge through the network, similarly to refusal vectors.
limitations: The unembedding matrix is only trained to operate on the final residual stream after all transformations; applying it to layer-6 activations extracts relevant information but may not precisely reflect the model’s underlying computation at that layer (nostalgebraist, 2020).

methods.name: Tuned Lens
methods.definition: Tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2025) addresses the vector space mismatch problem of logit lens by learning per-layer affine transformations that map intermediate activations to the output layer’s expected space
assumptions: The trade-off is that tuned lens requires training additional parameters (one affine transform per layer), but this is computationally cheap compared to other mechanistic methods.
applications: Tuned lens improves on basic logit lens by correcting for the fact that different layers operate in different representational spaces.
limitations: Because the mapping from intermediate representations to natural language may be too complex to be captured by an affine transformation, Patchscopes extends the paradigm of the logit lens and tuned lens by delegating the representation-to-text transformation to the language model itself

methods.name: Patchscopes
methods.definition: Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) leverages the expressive capacity of large language models to translate internal representations into natural-language explanations.
assumptions: Crucially, this approach relies on the model’s own learned and generalized text-generation capabilities to perform the transformation from internal activations to natural language.
limitations: A key limitation of Patchscopes is that injecting an external representation into an elicitation prompt can shift the model’s internal activations into an OOD regime.

Although the model may still successfully surface salient information from the patched representation, the decoding process can be degraded, and critical aspects of the original representation may be distorted or lost.

methods.name: LatentQA
methods.definition: LatentQA (Pan et al., 2024) formulates representation decoding as a supervised learning problem via Latent Interpretation Tuning (LIT), which fine-tunes an activation decoder to perform representation-to-text decoding.
assumptions: Both the control prompt and the (q, a) pair are generated by prompting an off-the-shelf proprietary language model (Pan et al., 2024).
Through LIT, the decoder is trained to directly ingest and process raw activation vectors.
applications: LatentQA addresses the OOD issue inherent in Patchscopes-style methods by explicitly finetuning the activation decoder on the representation-to-text decoding task.

Activation conditioning: Methods like LatentQA that condition on actual intermediate activations (rather than relying on the model to “remember” its computation) show improved faithfulness over pure prompting (Pan et al., 2024).
limitations: The central limitation of LatentQA lies in the generalizability of the learned representation-to-text decoder.

When the finetuning dataset D is insufficiently large or diverse, the decoder may overfit by memorizing superficial correspondences between representations and textual descriptions, rather than learning the underlying algorithmic transformation.

methods.name: Amnesic Probing
methods.definition: Building on this lineage, Elazar et al. (2021) introduced amnesic probing: after identifying a direction encoding property P, project it out of the representation and measure downstream task degradation.
evaluation: If performance degrades, the information was causally used. If performance is unchanged, the information was encoded but unused.
limitations: Limitations: Amnesic probing assumes the property is encoded in a single linear direction.
If encoding is distributed or nonlinear, projection may not fully remove the information, leading to false negatives (concluding information is unused when it is).

methods.name: Verbatim Data Attribution: OLMoTrace
methods.definition: Verbatim data attribution targets explicit memorization by identifying exact or near-exact matches between model outputs and training data, scaling this search across trillions of tokens via suffix arrays and infinite n-gram models.
assumptions: OLMoTrace scales this to trillions of tokens using a combination of FM-index, infini-gram models, and maximal matching span extraction (Liu et al., 2025a; 2024; Xu et al., 2025), making it less a data attribution method in the influence-function sense and more a retrieval tool for identifying memorized content.
applications: This process links LM outputs directly to the training corpus, enabling precise attribution of memorized content.
limitations: Verbatim attribution excels at factual memorization but struggles with compositional or synthesized outputs.

For tasks like translation, poetry, or reasoning, OLMoTrace can identify spans of text that appear in the training data, but these matches do not explain how the model combined information from multiple sources to produce the output (Park et al., 2023).

methods.name: Influence Functions (Gradient-Based Attribution)
methods.definition: Influence functions ask a counterfactual question: how would a model’s learned parameters change if we upweighted a training example (Koh & Liang, 2017)? Instead of expensive retraining, we estimate this via implicit differentiation (Grosse et al., 2023).
assumptions: The implicit function theorem assumes exact convergence and infinite perturbations.
Real neural networks violate both: training reaches saddle points, not true minima, and we retrain for only a few steps.
This equivalence allows practitioners to use Fisher information as a practical substitute: it’s more stable to compute and estimate from data than the true GGN.
evaluation: Observation: Influence functions successfully identify training documents that impacted the translation, even without exact verbatim matches.
applications: Training data attribution (TDA) answers a fundamental interpretability question: which training examples shaped specific model behaviors?
This enables identifying influential data, detecting train-test leakage, and understanding failure modes without retraining (Liu et al., 2025a; Park et al., 2023; Grosse et al., 2023).
limitations: However, fundamental challenges persist: approximation errors compound over optimization trajectories, random hyperparameters introduce variance across runs, and scaling to larger models remains memory-intensive.
Classical influence functions rely on inverting the Hessian of the loss landscape, which becomes ill-defined when the Fisher information matrix is degenerate.

methods.name: Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (KFAC)
methods.definition: KFAC is a parametric approximation to the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) of a neural network which supports efficient inversion.
limitations: KFAC works well but can underestimate curvature in low-variance directions due to finite sampling.

methods.name: Eigenvalue-Corrected KFAC (EK-FAC) and ASTRA
methods.definition: EK-FAC improves KFAC by correcting eigenvalues and is the method used by recent work scaling influence to LLMs (Grosse et al., 2023).
assumptions: An even more recent refinement, ASTRA (Wang et al., 2025a), uses EK-FAC as a preconditioner for Neumann series iterations, yielding higher-quality GGN-vector products with less hyperparameter tuning.
applications: These structured approaches make influence functions practical for models with billions of parameters.

methods.name: Approximate Unrolled Differentiation
methods.definition: Approximate unrolled differentiation (Bae et al., 2024) unfolds the optimization trajectory and backpropagates through training steps.
applications: This captures implicit bias of the optimizer and handles non-converged models, where classical influence functions struggle.
limitations: The tradeoff: higher computational cost than influence functions but better accuracy on modern, non-convex objectives.

methods.name: TRAK (Tracing with Randomly-projected After Kernel)
methods.definition: For large-scale attribution without retraining thousands of models, TRAK (Tracing with Randomly-projected After Kernel) provides a scalable alternative (Park et al., 2023).
evaluation: By avoiding prohibitive retraining costs, TRAK achieves attribution quality comparable to expensive retraining-based methods like datamodels (Ilyas et al., 2022) while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude.
applications: This enables application to large-scale models including vision transformers and billion-parameter language models, making fine-grained training data attribution tractable for modern deep learning (Park et al., 2023).

methods.name: TracIn
methods.definition: TracIn provides an efficient alternative to computing the full Hessian inverse by leveraging the training trajectory (Pruthi et al., 2020).
assumptions: This approach avoids Hessian computation entirely, instead accumulating dot products of gradients throughout training.
applications: TracIn is considerably cheaper than influence functions based on Hessian approximations, making it practical for large models.
Despite limitations, TracIn has enabled attribution studies on modern language models and provides a useful baseline for scalable influence estimation.
limitations: However, the approximation assumes that gradient trajectories during training encode sufficient information about final influence, an assumption that may break down in highly nonlinear settings or when training dynamics involve significant noise (Pruthi et al., 2020).

methods.name: Local Learning Coefficient (LLC)
methods.definition: In other words, it captures how many ways the parameters can vary locally without changing the loss value (Watanabe, 2009; Lau et al., 2023).
assumptions: Formally, the LLC is defined via the volume-scaling rate of the loss landscape near a minimum.
evaluation: Researchers have observed that transitions and critical points in the LLC often coincide with changes in internal network structure and functional behavior.
applications: Empirical estimators can track the LLC throughout training, providing a way to observe developmental changes in model structure (Lau et al., 2023; Hoogland et al., 2025).
Tracking these changes provides a quantitative way to study the emergence of structure during training without relying only on final performance metrics (Hoogland et al., 2025).

methods.name: Stagewise Influence and the Bayesian Influence Function (BIF)
methods.definition: Lee et al. (2025) propose a stagewise data attribution framework that extends classical influence methods to track the impact of training points throughout the learning process.
assumptions: Unlike classical influence functions that require Hessian inversion, the BIF measures influence through covariance estimation over the local posterior distribution.

This distributional approach is estimated via stochastic-gradient MCMC sampling, enabling scalable computation without explicit Hessian access while naturally capturing the geometry of singular loss landscapes.
evaluation: These predictions are further confirmed through leave-one-out retraining experiments that directly measure the effect of removing individual training examples at different stages of training.
applications: Token-level influence exhibits non-monotonic changes, including sudden peaks and sign reversals that align with known developmental milestones such as the formation of induction heads.

methods.name: Model Diffing
methods.definition: For two models, model diffing seeks to identify differences in features or circuits between them. These differences may consist of features or circuits that are exclusive to one model, or of differences in how shared features or circuits are used.
assumptions: SAEs can be applied to model-diffing when inputs from different models have the same dimension.
To diff closed-weight models, it is desirable to develop model diffing tools that just rely on API access.
evaluation: Benchmarked against an SAE-based baseline, the LLM-based method matches it on many dimensions while surfacing more abstract, behaviour-level differences.
applications: This makes it important to monitor features and circuits that have been introduced or amplified during this process to prevent unsafe models from being deployed.

Model diffing has been applied to assess the effect of finetuning (Minder et al., 2025; Lindsey et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Aranguri & McGrath, 2025) and distillation (Baek & Tegmark, 2025), to track differences across model architectures (Thasarathan et al., 2025; Jiralerspong & Bricken, 2025), and to study the evolution of concepts during pretraining (Bayazit et al., 2025; Ge et al., 2025).
limitations: Dictionary learning methods for model-diffing risk falsely identifying model-exclusive features (Minder et al., 2025; Jiralerspong & Bricken, 2025).

During finetuning, the direction representing some feature can rotate, and dictionary learning methods currently cannot distinguish between features that are introduced via finetuning as opposed to merely represented differently.
Thus, supposedly model-exclusive features should be regarded as hypotheses that need further validation.

methods.name: Representation Alignment and Convergent Learning (SVCCA, PWCCA, CKA)
methods.definition: An earlier line of work compared internal representations across models by measuring statistical similarity between neurons or subspaces, using correlation or mutual information (Li et al., 2015), canonical correlation–based methods such as SVCCA and PWCCA (Raghu et al., 2017; Morcos et al., 2018b), or kernel-based alignment metrics like CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019).
applications: This literature primarily aims to characterize convergent learning: whether independently trained models (often only differing by weight initialisation) learn similar representations up to permutation, rotation, or linear reparameterization.
limitations: In contrast to model diffing as defined here, these methods typically focus on representational similarity rather than on identifying features or circuits that are introduced, amplified, or repurposed by a specific training intervention.

methods.name: Causal Tracing (Knowledge Localization)
methods.definition: Causal tracing identifies which attention heads or MLP directions are causally responsible for particular facts or reasoning tasks by measuring how intervening on those components affects output behavior (Meng et al., 2022).
applications: Once knowledge is attributed to specific model components via localization techniques like causal tracing, mechanistic approaches enable direct parameter modification.
limitations: Knowledge is often distributed across many parameters rather than concentrated in isolated components, particularly in large overparameterized models where redundancy is common.
Consequently, knowledge localization is most useful when combined with mechanistic analysis of how multiple components interact to implement computation.

methods.name: Representation Engineering and Steering (Steering Vectors)
methods.definition: Representation engineering aims to control model behavior by intervening directly in activation space rather than modifying weights. A prominent class of methods, generally defined as activation steering, biases model outputs by adding carefully chosen directions to intermediate activations—most commonly the residual stream—during inference.
assumptions: These interventions are lightweight, require no retraining, and are therefore attractive for rapid behavioral control in deployed systems.
In practice, v is estimated by contrasting activations associated with different behaviors, e.g., taking differences of class-conditional means
evaluation: Such intervention-based evaluations directly measure the causal effects of extracted features on model outputs.

Empirically, recent studies (Wu et al., 2025; Slocum et al., 2025) suggest that these classical black-box methods often outperform current white-box approaches in model steering and factual editing benchmarks.
applications: Despite their simplicity, steering vectors reliably induce behaviors like improved helpfulness, refusal suppression, or stylistic changes (Rimsky et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2025).
Researchers were able to identify and deploy the steering vector that suppresses this awareness, allowing its safety to be evaluated.
Their primary advantage is computational efficiency (no retraining required), methodological simplicity, and inference-time reversibility.
limitations: First, they often fail to generalize across distribution shifts: a vector derived for one task may degrade in another.
As a result, steering remains primarily a behavioral tool rather than a mechanistic one.
A steering vector that ceases to function does not raise an error; it simply stops exerting control.
Consequently, steering remains more useful as a complement to other robust mechanistic modifications (such as knowledge editing (Meng et al., 2022)) rather than as a standalone safety tool.

methods.name: Optimization-Based Steering
methods.definition: Beyond closed-form constructions, steering directions can be obtained by directly optimizing objectives over activations—maximizing task performance or suppressing undesired outputs under intervention.
limitations: These optimization-based approaches allow greater flexibility and adapt to complex, non-linear objectives, but incur higher computational cost (Dunefsky & Cohan, 2025; Oozeer et al., 2025a).

methods.name: Concept Erasure via PISCES
methods.definition: PISCES (Precise In-Parameter Concept Erasure in Large Language Models) (Gur-Arieh et al., 2025b) addresses this limitation through a three-stage methodology.
assumptions: Stage 1 – Feature Disentanglement and Identification: Use SAEs with feature explanations (via Automated Interpretability pipeline) to disentangle and identify features associated with the target concept c (e.g., “biological toxins”)
evaluation: Result: “Surgical” erasure that reduced accuracy on prohibited concepts to near-chance levels (7.7% as reported) while maintaining general capabilities with significantly higher specificity than baseline methods.
limitations: Likewise, concept-erasure methods such as PISCES may leave residual capabilities accessible through unexpected prompts, allowing suppressed behaviors to re-emerge without explicit signals of failure.

Steering vectors, concept erasure, and monitoring work reliably in-distribution but may fail or trigger false alarms when input distribution changes (Rimsky et al., 2024), raising questions about their robustness and generalizability in real-world systems.

methods.name: Knowledge Editing via Localization (ROME, MEMIT)
methods.definition: For example, ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) serve as practical tools for component-based knowledge editing: they apply localized rank-one updates to parameter matrices identified as storing particular factual knowledge, achieving targeted removal of harmful knowledge with minimal collateral damage.
assumptions: Once knowledge is attributed to specific model components via localization techniques like causal tracing, mechanistic approaches enable direct parameter modification.
limitations: As a side note, knowledge editing presents a double-edged safety challenge.
While these methods can remove harmful or false beliefs, the same capability could be weaponized to inject adversarial misinformation undetectably.

Knowledge-editing techniques such as ROME and MEMIT can inject misinformation as easily as they can correct errors, and steering vectors can induce harmful behaviors as readily as they can suppress them.

methods.name: Mechanistic Monitoring
methods.definition: Behavioral monitoring watches outputs; mechanistic monitoring watches internals.
assumptions: Methods for achieving mechanistic monitoring include, but are not limited to, layer-wise monitoring (using linear probes to classify if malicious intent is encoded in a layer representation), feature-wise monitoring (alerting when unexpected SAE features activate), and circuit-wise monitoring (tracking causal effects among attention heads, MLPs, or features).
applications: The advantages of mechanistic monitoring over behavioral monitoring are several: deceptive reasoning may not manifest behaviorally but may be detectable mechanistically.
limitations: However, technical challenges also exist, such as determining what to monitor (millions of features), false positives (legitimate reasoning that looks suspicious), and adaptive evasion (models learning to hide suspicious activity if monitored).
Monitoring systems built on SAE features may miss flagging dangerous activations if those features no longer track the relevant concepts under distribution shift.

hypotheses.name: The Linear Representation Hypothesis
hypotheses.definition: The linear representation hypothesis claims that directions in the activation space are the fundamental units of representation.

hypotheses.name: The Superposition Hypothesis
hypotheses.definition: The superposition hypothesis says that for each layer of a trained model there are more features than nodes.

hypotheses.name: The Privileged Access Hypothesis
hypotheses.definition: A model used to interpret itself can, under appropriate elicitation, access internal variables and intermediate computations that are not reliably recoverable from external behavioral analysis alone, providing a comparative advantage as an interpreter of its own behavior

hypotheses.name: The Universality and Platonic Representation Hypotheses
hypotheses.definition: Independently trained models on similar tasks tend to develop similar internal computational structures. These representations often approximate a task-determined canonical form (Huh et al., 2024; Olah et al., 2020).
